topStories.headline: Voters Say No to Prop G — Sunset Dunes Stays Car-Free for Good
topStories.dek: San Francisco rejected the third ballot measure in six years to restore weekday vehicle access to the former Great Highway, with roughly 63% voting against Prop G.
topStories.body:
Sunset Dunes will remain a full-time, car-free coastal park after San Francisco voters decisively defeated Proposition G on November 3, rejecting the measure by a margin of roughly 63 to 37 percent. The measure would have reopened the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles on weekdays while keeping it closed on weekends and holidays.

It was the third time voters have weighed in on the fate of the Pacific-hugging roadway since 2022. In 2024, Proposition K passed with 55 percent of the vote, permanently closing the highway to cars and paving the way for Sunset Dunes Park. Prop G qualified for the November ballot after supporters gathered more than 15,000 signatures in an attempt to partially reverse that decision. Voters said no — and by a wider margin than the 2024 vote that created the park in the first place.

District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong, who backed the measure, said in a post-election statement that he respects the voters' decision and that his focus going forward will be on addressing the neighborhood impacts of the permanent closure.

A precinct-by-precinct breakdown showed a sharp geographic divide: much of the Sunset, Parkside, and Richmond voted in favor of reopening the highway, while central, eastern, and southeastern San Francisco provided the decisive opposition. Despite strong local support for Prop G, the citywide verdict was not close.

With a simultaneous ballot measure making it considerably harder to place future citizen initiatives before voters, advocates on both sides said November 3 is likely the last word on the Great Highway for years to come. The saga traces back to 2020, when a pandemic-era pilot first closed the road on weekends.

topStories.headline: El Niño Could Push Seawater Onto Sunset Dunes This Winter, City Warns
topStories.dek: Record-high tides are expected at Ocean Beach this season, and city officials say they are preparing for potential flooding all the way to the edge of the former highway roadway.
topStories.body:
City officials and coastal scientists are sounding early warnings about Ocean Beach as an El Niño-driven winter approaches. High tides are expected to reach record levels in San Francisco, with the possibility that seawater could push all the way across the sand and up to the edge of Sunset Dunes Park — the former Great Highway roadway.

Chase Davenport, director of the Ocean Beach Institute, was on the beach in late October taking baseline measurements to compare against anticipated water levels this winter. He noted that the beach is currently at its widest point, meaning it has more visible sand now than it will during most of the colder months ahead. Mayor Daniel Lurie said at a press conference that city authorities are prepared to respond to flooding at Ocean Beach and several other waterfront areas around San Francisco.

The potential for flooding adds a new practical dimension to the question of how to manage the city's western shoreline now that the closure of the Great Highway to vehicles has been settled at the ballot box. A separate long-term coastal resilience effort — the Ocean Beach Climate Change Resilience Project — has already been pushed back once this year and is now not expected to begin construction until late 2029, with the full project not expected to be complete until 2033 at the earliest.

topStories.headline: Sunset Social Club Wants to Throw 400 Block Parties at Once This Spring
topStories.dek: Two Sunset residents are organizing a neighborhood-wide celebration they're calling the Sunset Wave — hundreds of simultaneous block parties intended to bridge the community's generational and political divides.
topStories.body:
A new effort is underway to stitch together a neighborhood that has spent several years fighting over the Great Highway. Two Sunset residents, Sandi Lam Harder and Josh Nesbit, have launched the Sunset Social Club and are organizing what may be the city's largest-ever block party event: roughly 400 simultaneous neighborhood gatherings planned for a single spring day.

The founders, who operate out of a former church in the Sunset, describe the event — which they are calling the Sunset Wave — as a way to bridge the generational and political divide between the neighborhood's historically blue-collar longtime residents and a newer wave of younger arrivals. About 350 people have already signed up as club members, and the organizers plan to recruit block hosts from that group first. Anyone can sign up to host, however, and multiple hosts on the same block are welcome.

The San Francisco Standard reported on the effort on November 1, noting that organizers see a spring fresh-start theme as particularly fitting for the Sunset given the years of political turbulence surrounding Sunset Dunes. No specific date has been announced yet, but the founders described the target as a spring equinox celebration.

moreNews.headline: All SF Libraries Close for Veterans Day on Wednesday, November 11
moreNews.body: The San Francisco Public Library system, including the Sunset Branch at 1305 18th Avenue in the Inner Sunset, will be closed on Wednesday, November 11 in observance of Veterans Day. Regular hours resume Thursday, November 12.

moreNews.headline: Sunset Rec Center Gets New Goalphers to Expand Youth Soccer Access
moreNews.body: SF Recreation and Parks recently installed Goalphers — rebounding goal training devices — at Sunset Recreation Center on Lawton Street in the Outer Sunset. The department said the new equipment is intended to increase access to soccer for neighborhood kids who use the center.

restaurants.name: Maggie & Mac's

restaurants.name: Arizmendi Bakery

restaurants.name: The Red Tail
restaurants.description: Stylish wine bar on Irving Street open until 11 p.m., filling a long-standing gap in the neighborhood's after-dinner scene.

restaurants.name: Yancy's Saloon
restaurants.description: Old-school dive bar with dart boards, multiple TV screens for sports, and a spacious interior beloved by neighborhood regulars for decades.

restaurants.name: Sunset Cantina

restaurants.name: Andytown Coffee Roasters

restaurants.name: Dumpling Kitchen
restaurants.description: Beloved Parkside dumpling institution on Taraval with consistently long waits for its fresh, flavorful handmade dumplings.

restaurants.name: Golden Boy Pizza
restaurants.description: Parkside outpost of the legendary 1978 North Beach pizzeria, serving thick focaccia-based square slices with toppings like garlic-clam and pesto vegetable.

restaurants.name: Galinette

restaurants.name: New Taraval Cafe

hotels.name: Motel 6 San Francisco – Great Highway
